strengths: The paper introduces a clear and interesting new problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading. This is a meaningful extension beyond prior work on procedural reading-task classification.

The use of the OneStop eye-tracking dataset is well motivated, and the critical-span structure enables a thoughtful evaluation split between easier different-span discrimination and harder same-span discrimination.

The experimental protocol considers generalization to new participants, new texts, and both, which is important for this non-i.i.d. setting. The paper also reports confidence intervals and mixed-effects significance tests.

The strongest discriminative model, RoBERTEye-Fixations, achieves consistent above-chance performance, including on same-span questions, suggesting that eye movements contain some fine-grained information about reader goals.

The paper is generally clearly written, with useful appendices describing model adaptations, features, prompts, hyperparameters, and additional results. Ethical concerns around privacy and consent are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The main claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. The task is framed as decoding arbitrary open-ended goals, but the primary successful result is a constrained three-way selection among known candidate questions from a dataset with exactly three questions per paragraph.

The strongest results are moderate: 49.3% versus 33% on three-way selection and 57.3% versus 50% on same-span selection. These are interesting but not yet compelling enough to support the broader application-oriented claims.

A key missing control is a rigorous no-eye-movement or shuffled-eye-movement ablation for the discriminative models. Since the models receive the paragraph and candidate questions, it is important to quantify exactly how much of the gain comes from gaze rather than textual/question priors, architecture biases, or dataset regularities.

The generative contribution is weak. DalEye-LLaVA is essentially at chance for selection, and DalEye-Llama underperforms the discriminative model. Reconstruction generalizes well mainly to new participants when the text was seen during training; on new texts it is close to or worse than several baselines on important metrics.
The New Text & Participant regime is small within each split, making that most realistic generalization condition less convincing despite aggregation across folds.

The evaluation of reconstruction relies heavily on heuristic metrics and an automatic QA model filtered to questions it answers correctly. This is creative, but it does not fully establish that generated questions recover the reader's actual goal.

The paper would benefit from more direct analyses of what gaze patterns the models use, calibration/error analysis by question type and critical-span overlap, and robustness tests across readers or texts with different characteristics.
Reproducibility is only partial: the public dataset is cited and many details are provided, but code/model release and exact preprocessing details are not clearly established in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper poses an interesting and relatively novel problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading, including both multiple-choice goal selection and open-ended question reconstruction.
The use of the OneStop eye-tracking dataset is well motivated, and the paper carefully distinguishes generalization to new participants, new texts, and both new participants and texts.
The manuscript is readable and includes several model families, including simple reading-time baselines, adapted discriminative eye-movement models, and generative LLM-based variants.
The best discriminative model reports clear gains over chance on the main selection task, especially for distinguishing questions tied to different critical spans.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not strong enough for a top-tier AI venue. The best overall selection accuracy is only 49.3% for a 3-way task with 33% chance, and the most interesting same-critical-span setting reaches only 57.3% versus 50% chance. This is statistically significant but modest, and the paper sometimes presents it as stronger evidence of fine-grained goal decoding than the numbers justify.

The open-ended reconstruction results are weak under the most important generalization regimes. For new texts and new text plus participant, DalEye-Llama has near-zero question-word/category kappa and is beaten by simple baselines on several metrics, including same-span human questions on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy. This substantially undercuts the claim of meaningful progress toward free-form reconstruction.

The strongest model is an adapted existing discriminative model, while the proposed generative models are either near chance for selection or weak for reconstruction outside seen texts. As a result, the modeling contribution is limited relative to the task proposal.

Important ablations are missing. The paper needs trained text-only, eye-only, shuffled-eye, participant-ID, and no-word-property controls for the discriminative models to establish that gains truly come from goal-specific eye movements rather than dataset, participant, text, or feature artifacts.

The evaluation is based on a single dataset with only 162 paragraphs and 486 questions, all from one experimental paradigm. This makes broad claims about arbitrary open-ended reading goals, real-time assistive applications, and general cognitive-state decoding premature.

The reconstruction metrics are imperfect and in places hard to interpret. QA accuracy depends on a separate RoBERTa QA model and is evaluated only on questions it answers correctly; BLEU/BERTScore reward lexical overlap with span-related questions; GPT-4o category labeling adds another model-dependent evaluation layer.

The paper lacks practical analysis of deployment-relevant factors such as calibration, per-user variability, robustness to noisier commodity eye trackers, latency, amount of per-text/per-reader data needed, and failure modes for readers outside the dataset population.

Ethical risks are acknowledged but not deeply handled. Inferring users' goals from gaze data is privacy-sensitive, and the paper's discussion of consent, misuse, demographic bias, and safeguards remains fairly high level.

strengths: Introduces a novel and interesting problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading, including both candidate selection and free-form reconstruction formulations.

Uses a well-motivated public eye-tracking dataset with many readers, paragraphs, and manually annotated critical spans, enabling meaningful evaluation of generalization to new participants and new texts.

The experimental design is thoughtful: the paper distinguishes different-span and same-span cases, uses cross-validation, reports confidence intervals, and evaluates several model families from simple reading-time heuristics to adapted neural eye-movement models and generative LLMs.
Results are encouraging, especially for RoBERTEye-Fixations, which substantially exceeds chance on three-way selection and remains above chance even in the harder same-critical-span condition.

The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to psycholinguistics and prior eye-movement modeling work. The ethical discussion appropriately flags consent, privacy, and reliability concerns.
weaknesses: The central claims about arbitrary/open-ended goal decoding are somewhat stronger than the evidence. The strongest results are for selecting among only three known candidate questions for a paragraph; the genuinely free-form reconstruction results are much weaker, especially for new texts.

The evaluation would benefit from stronger controls and ablations. In particular, the paper lacks neural no-eye, shuffled-eye, averaged-eye, and paragraph/question-only controls for the discriminative models, making it harder to isolate how much performance comes specifically from individual gaze behavior rather than text/question priors, architecture, or dataset regularities.

Generalization to new texts is only moderately convincing. Selection performance drops in the more difficult same-span setting, and reconstruction metrics for new text/new participant settings are close to or worse than several baselines on important measures.

The generative models are not very successful relative to the discriminative models: DalEye-LLaVA is near chance for selection, and DalEye-Llama’s reconstruction quality appears heavily dependent on whether the paragraph was seen during training.

The dataset and task setup are narrow: all experiments use one English dataset, one reading-comprehension paradigm, short paragraphs, and pre-existing human-written questions. This limits the strength of claims about real-world information-seeking behavior or assistive/educational deployment.

Some evaluation choices for reconstruction are heuristic and imperfect. BLEU/BERTScore and QA-model accuracy can reward lexical or answer-span overlap rather than faithful recovery of the reader’s actual goal. Human evaluation of generated questions would strengthen the conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete as written: the public dataset is mentioned, but code release, trained checkpoints, exact split files, and implementation details for all adapted models are not clearly committed to in the manuscript.

strengths: Introduces a novel and meaningful task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, moving beyond prior binary/procedural reading-goal classification.
Uses a well-motivated public eye-tracking dataset with hundreds of questions, critical-span annotations, and a careful split design covering new participants, new texts, and both.

Evaluation is comparatively thorough: discriminative selection, open-ended reconstruction, multiple baselines, confidence intervals, mixed-effects significance testing, feature ablations, and cognitively interpretable analyses.

The best discriminative model shows consistent above-chance performance, including generalization to new texts and a harder same-critical-span condition, supporting the core claim that gaze contains goal-relevant signal.
The paper is clearly written, well situated in psycholinguistics and NLP, and includes useful implementation, hyperparameter, ethics, and reproducibility details.
weaknesses: The phrase 'arbitrary open-ended goals' is somewhat overstated: the setting is limited to 486 prewritten reading-comprehension questions, with only three possible questions per paragraph in the selection task.
The strongest selection result is moderate rather than decisive: 49.3% three-way accuracy and 57.3% same-span accuracy, so practical real-time goal decoding remains far from established.

Goal reconstruction evidence is less convincing than selection evidence. Improvements over text-only baselines in the New Text setting are often small, metric-dependent, and sometimes absent, while automatic metrics such as BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy are imperfect proxies for semantic reconstruction quality.

The New Participant reconstruction regime may partly reward memorization of text-question associations, since the same paragraph/questions appear in training; Gemini few-shot also uses examples from the same paragraph in that regime, which weakens claims about decoding from eye movements rather than recalling plausible questions.

Scope is narrow: English-only, lab-based reading, one dataset, short paragraphs, adult native speakers, and high-quality eye tracking. Generalization to web reading, mobile devices, L2 readers, accessibility populations, or noisier gaze sensors is not demonstrated.
Some reproducibility aspects depend on commercial/closed models and APIs, including GPT-4o-mini fine-tuning and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview, which may be hard to reproduce exactly.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and underexplored problem: whether readers' information-seeking goals can be inferred from eye movements during reading. This is a meaningful cognitive modeling question with plausible relevance to assistive and educational applications.

The experimental setup is relatively careful for the available data: the authors distinguish new-participant, new-text, and new-text-and-participant regimes; report confidence intervals and mixed-effects significance tests; and include both selection and generation formulations.

The best discriminative model shows consistent above-chance performance, especially for distinguishing different critical spans, and the analysis linking model performance to reading time inside vs. outside the critical span is cognitively interpretable and useful.
The paper includes several baselines, ablations, appendix details, and ethical considerations, which improves transparency relative to many papers in this area.
weaknesses: The central framing of decoding 'arbitrary' or 'open-ended' goals is substantially overstated. The main selection task is choosing among only three known questions for a paragraph, with a dataset where the possible questions and critical spans are predefined. This is much narrower than open-ended goal decoding from eye movements.

Much of the apparent success is driven by coarse localization of the critical span rather than decoding the precise question. The different-span accuracy is reasonably strong, but the same-span result is only 57.3% vs. 50% chance, indicating weak evidence for fine-grained goal inference.

The goal reconstruction results are not very convincing in the hardest and most relevant settings. Performance drops sharply for new texts, gains over text-only baselines are often small or absent, and human same-critical-span distractor questions outperform or match models on some semantic/similarity measures.

The generative evaluation is heavily heuristic. BLEU, BERTScore, question-word accuracy, and LLM-derived question categories only weakly establish that the generated question captures the reader's actual goal. The QA-based metric is indirect and evaluated only on the subset answerable by a RoBERTa QA model.

The New Participant regime is potentially much easier than the paper's motivating use case because the text and all candidate questions have appeared in training. In this setting, reconstruction can partly reduce to memorizing paragraph-specific questions and using gaze to select among them.

The New Text & Participant regime, arguably the cleanest test of practical generalization, is very small per split and receives limited discussion. This weakens claims about deployment or broad generalization.

The modeling contribution is limited: the paper mostly adapts existing eye-movement/text models and LLM fine-tuning pipelines to a new task. The strongest contribution is the task formulation and empirical study rather than a new AI method.

Some claims about future real-time assistance and decoding reader goals are stronger than what the reported accuracy supports, especially given the controlled lab setting, known passages/questions, and moderate same-span performance.

strengths: The paper tackles a novel and interesting problem: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading. This is a meaningful extension beyond prior work that mostly distinguishes broad reading modes or reader traits.

The experimental design is well matched to the question. OneStop provides multiple questions per passage, annotated critical spans, and repeated readings across participants, enabling evaluation across new participants, new texts, and both.

The evaluation is unusually careful for this kind of multimodal/cognitive modeling work: the paper reports multiple task variants, confidence intervals, mixed-effects significance tests, validation/test breakdowns, feature ablations, and several reconstruction metrics.

The discriminative results are convincing. RoBERTEye-Fixations substantially outperforms chance and simpler baselines, including in the harder same-critical-span setting, suggesting that eye movements contain signal beyond coarse location-of-attention cues.

The cognitive analysis linking model performance to interpretable reading behavior is a strong component. The finding that performance improves when readers spend more time in the critical span and less time outside it provides useful scientific insight rather than only benchmark numbers.
The paper is clearly written, well positioned with respect to psycholinguistics and NLP eye-tracking work, and includes substantial implementation and prompt details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central framing as decoding open-ended or arbitrary goals is stronger than the empirical setup supports. The data contains only three pre-authored candidate questions per paragraph, with two tied to the same critical span, so the work is still constrained by a specific QA design rather than truly open-ended reader goals.

The absolute performance, especially in the most challenging settings, is modest. Same-span selection reaches about 57% versus 50% chance, and new-text reconstruction often provides only small gains over text-only baselines, so the practical utility remains preliminary.

The generative reconstruction results are less compelling than the selection results. Automatic metrics such as BLEU, BERTScore, question-word accuracy, and QA-model accuracy only imperfectly measure whether the inferred goal is semantically correct, and human evaluation of generated questions would strengthen the claims.

Some gains may reflect dataset/task regularities rather than robust goal decoding. In the New Participant setting, models have seen the text and possible questions during training, and the strong performance of text-only baselines indicates that language priors and passage/question distributions explain a nontrivial portion of the results.

The feature ablations suggest that much of the performance may come from fixation order aligned with word embeddings and possibly redundant or coarse features; the paper could more sharply isolate what information is uniquely contributed by eye movements beyond text, reading time, and task structure.

The dataset scope is narrow: English Guardian-style paragraphs, native adult readers, controlled lab eye tracking, and short reading-comprehension questions. Generalization to other domains, languages, devices, longer documents, or naturalistic information needs is not established.

Reproducibility is partly limited by reliance on commercial models and future-dated/proprietary systems such as Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and GPT-4o-mini fine-tuning, though the main discriminative models appear more reproducible.
